title: He Had Money, Morality, and Influence. He Still Walked Away From Jesus Sad.
paragraphs: He Had Money, Morality, and Influence. He Still Walked Away From Jesus Sad.
The Rich Young Ruler did almost everything religious people admire—and still discovered that being close to Jesus is not the same as belonging completely to Jesus.
There is something terrifying about a man running toward Jesus… only to eventually walk away from Him.
Not cursing Him.
Not mocking Him.
Not denying that He was good.
Just walking away.
Sad.
That may be one of the most uncomfortable scenes in the Gospels because the man does not look like someone we would expect to be spiritually lost.
He is not presented as a public scandal.
He is not the thief hanging on a cross.
He is not the woman whose reputation entered the room before she did.
He is not the tax collector everyone despised.
By the standards of respectable society, this man appears to have almost everything right.
He is young.
He has wealth.
Luke calls him a ruler.
He appears morally serious.
And when Jesus comes near, Mark tells us something remarkable:
“καὶ προσδραμὼν εἷς καὶ γονυπετήσας αὐτόν…”
A man came running and knelt before Him.
That matters.
This was not casual curiosity.
Imagine the scene.
A wealthy, influential man sees Jesus leaving. Something inside him refuses to let the moment pass. Dignity gives way to desperation. He runs. He drops to his knees.
Then comes the question:
“Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
It sounds like the beginning of a beautiful conversion story.
But before this conversation is finished, the same man who ran toward Jesus will walk away from Jesus.
And perhaps the most haunting question in the story is not simply why he walked away.
It is this:
What could Jesus ask you to surrender that would make you do the same?
Because it is possible to run toward Jesus while still carrying something you have already decided He cannot have.
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
That is where it finds us.

The account appears in Matthew 19:16–30, Mark 10:17–31, and Luke 18:18–30. The familiar description “rich young ruler” comes from reading those accounts together: Matthew identifies him as young, Luke calls him a ruler, and all three emphasize his wealth.
He comes asking about eternal life, and Jesus brings the conversation into the territory of God’s commandments.
The man answers with astonishing confidence.
“Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.”
Think about that.
He has morality.
He has discipline.
He has religious knowledge.
He has social standing.
He has money.
And apparently he still knows that something is missing.
There are people reading this who understand that feeling more than they want to admit.
You learned how to behave.
You learned Christian language.
You know when to say “God is good.”
You know which verses to post.
You may attend church, give money, avoid obvious scandals, take care of your family, work hard, and try to be a decent person.
People may even look at your life and think,
That person is blessed.
But late at night, when there is nobody left to impress, a quieter question sometimes rises:
Why does my soul still feel like it is negotiating with God?
That is the danger of respectable Christianity.
A person can clean the outside of life so thoroughly that nobody notices there is still a throne inside the heart occupied by something other than Christ.
And Jesus knows exactly where that throne is.
Mark gives us a detail so beautiful that it changes the emotional temperature of the entire encounter.
“ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν.”
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Do not rush past that.
Jesus is about to say the sentence that exposes the man’s deepest attachment.
And Mark tells us first that Jesus loved him.
The confrontation came from love.
The exposure came from love.
The demand came from love.
Jesus was not trying to humiliate a wealthy man.
He was uncovering the rival that owned him.
Then Jesus said:
“ἕν σε ὑστερεῖ…”
“You lack one thing.”
One thing.
The man had accumulated so much, yet Jesus could see the poverty hidden underneath the abundance.
Then came the command:
“Go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me.”
This passage must be handled carefully.

Jesus is not teaching that people purchase eternal life by donating enough money. Scripture does not teach salvation by charitable achievement. Salvation is by God’s grace, received through faith, not earned by works.

Nor does Scripture give a universal command requiring every Christian in every circumstance to dispose of every possession. The New Testament includes believers who possessed homes and resources, and it repeatedly teaches generosity, stewardship, freedom from greed, and care for those in need.
But none of that makes Jesus’ command to this particular man less radical.
Jesus placed His finger precisely where this man’s allegiance was divided.
The man asked what he needed.
Jesus showed him what owned him.
His wealth was not merely something sitting in his hands.
It had reached his heart.
This is why the story is bigger than money.
For one person, the rival may be wealth.
For another, it is a relationship they know is pulling them away from Christ.
For another, pornography hidden behind a password.
For another, applause.
A career.
A reputation.
Bitterness.
Control.
Sexual sin.
Comfort.
Pride.
A secret habit.
A public image.
Even ministry can become an idol when being seen serving Jesus becomes more precious than Jesus Himself.
An idol is not merely a statue someone bows before.
It is anything we refuse to place beneath the lordship of Christ.
And sometimes we discover what we worship only when God touches it.
We sing, “I surrender all,” until Jesus points toward the thing we mentally excluded from the word all.
That is what happened on the road.
Jesus did not merely discuss the man’s possessions.
He revealed his master.
Then Mark uses a word that almost lets you see the man’s face change:
“στυγνάσας.”
His expression fell.
He became gloomy, shocked, disheartened.
Then:
“ἀπῆλθεν λυπούμενος.”
He went away grieving.
Why?
“ἦν γὰρ ἔχων κτήματα πολλά.”
Because he had many possessions.
He arrived running.
He left grieving.
He arrived kneeling.
He left unwilling to surrender.
He wanted eternal life.
He wanted Jesus’ answer.
But when the answer threatened his treasure, he chose the treasure.
And this is where the story becomes frighteningly personal.
He did not walk away because Jesus failed to love him.
Jesus loved him.
He walked away because the love of Jesus confronted another love he was unwilling to release.
Read that again slowly.
Jesus loved him enough to tell him the truth that could cost Jesus the man’s approval.
That is real love.
Modern Christianity can be tempted to imagine love as affirmation without confrontation.
Jesus refuses that definition.
Sometimes Christ loves us by comforting us.
Sometimes Christ loves us by exposing us.
Sometimes His mercy feels like arms around the wounded.
Sometimes His mercy feels like light entering a locked room.
Both are love.
The Rich Young Ruler wanted assurance.
Jesus offered discipleship.
He wanted to know what could be added to his life.
Jesus exposed what needed to lose its throne.
He seems to have approached eternal life as another possession to acquire.
He already had status.
He already had morality.
He already had wealth.
Perhaps eternal life could become one more treasure in an impressive collection.
But Jesus cannot simply be added to a life whose throne remains occupied.
Christ does not come merely to become another item in our collection.
He comes as Lord.
That word matters.
Lord.
κύριος.
The Christian confession is not merely that Jesus is useful, inspiring, therapeutic, or spiritually comforting.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And lordship reaches into bank accounts.
Bedrooms.
Phones.
Relationships.
Ambitions.
Private thoughts.
Public reputations.
The parts of us nobody else sees.
This does not mean Christians become perfect overnight.
It means we stop defending our rebellion as though Jesus has no right to touch it.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and protecting it.
Between falling and refusing to get up.
Between weakness that cries for grace and rebellion that demands permission.
The Gospel does not say, “Fix yourself so Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
You cannot save yourself.
And Jesus came for sinners who cannot.
After the wealthy man leaves, Jesus tells His disciples how difficult it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God. The disciples are astonished.
Then they ask the question underneath every human attempt at salvation:
“Who then can be saved?”
Jesus looks at them and answers:
“With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.”
There is the Gospel breaking through the story.
Impossible with man.
Possible with God.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot behave your way into resurrection.
You cannot build a résumé impressive enough to make God owe you heaven.
You cannot give enough money, attend enough services, perform enough religious acts, or accumulate enough moral accomplishments to erase your guilt.
You need something you cannot manufacture.
Grace.
You need Someone you cannot replace.
Jesus.
The Rich Young Ruler had asked, in effect, “What can I do?”
Jesus eventually brings the conversation to the terrifying and liberating reality:
Human beings cannot save themselves.
That is why the cross matters.
Jesus did not come merely to make morally impressive people slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
The scandal of Christianity is that the respectable moralist and the publicly disgraced sinner ultimately stand in need of the same Savior.
Different histories.
Different wounds.
Different temptations.
Same need for grace.
At the cross, Jesus bears sin.
In His resurrection, death is defeated.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not to purchase mercy but to repent and believe.
Repentance is not payment for grace.
It is the turning of the heart toward the God who gives grace.
Faith is not another achievement we wave before God.
It is the empty hand receiving Christ.
And perhaps this is why the story hurts so much.
The man was standing in front of the Treasure he could never purchase.
Yet he walked away because he could not imagine releasing the treasures he already possessed.
He had money.
But Jesus offered treasure in heaven.
He had status.
But Jesus offered discipleship.
He had moral accomplishments.
But Jesus offered grace.
He had possessions.
But Jesus said:
“Follow Me.”
And he walked away.
We are not told that Jesus chased him down and renegotiated the terms.
Jesus did not shout after him:
“Wait! Keep the idol. Just add Me to it.”
He let the man feel the weight of his choice.
That silence should disturb us.
Because there are moments when the most dangerous thing God can allow is for us to keep choosing what we demanded.
Some people want Jesus as Savior from hell while resisting Jesus as Lord of life.
They want forgiveness without repentance.
Comfort without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
A cross that saves them, but never crosses out anything they worship.
But biblical grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace forgives us and begins transforming us.
Titus says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness.
Paul says that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
The Gospel does not merely change our destination after death.
It begins changing our allegiance now.
And here is where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Some scandals are visible.
Everybody knows.
The affair.
The addiction.
The arrest.
The divorce.
The collapse.
The betrayal.
The public failure.
But some scandals wear expensive clothes.
Some scandals have excellent reputations.
Some scandals sit quietly in church.
Some scandals know Bible verses.
Some scandals give to charity.
Some scandals look morally admirable while privately telling Jesus:
“You can have everything except this.”
The Rich Young Ruler’s scandal was not that he possessed wealth.
The deeper scandal was that when Jesus exposed the competing loyalty of his heart, he preferred what he possessed to the One standing before him.
Yet even here, grace remains breathtakingly close.
Remember the sentence Mark refused to leave out:
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Before the man surrendered, Jesus loved him.
While exposing him, Jesus loved him.
Knowing what he would choose, Jesus loved him.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without pretending.
You can stop hiding because Christ already knows what is behind the door.
He knows the browser history.
He knows the bank statement.
He knows the resentment.
He knows the secret relationship.
He knows why you need everybody to admire you.
He knows what you are afraid to lose.
He knows the thing you hope He never mentions.
And still the crucified and risen Christ calls sinners to Himself.
So ask the question you may have avoided for years:
What is my “one thing”?
What makes your heart tense when surrender is mentioned?
What do you repeatedly justify even though Scripture keeps confronting it?
What loss seems more unbearable than distance from Jesus?
What are you afraid Christ might ask you to put down?
Your answer may reveal more about your worship than a hundred songs ever could.
Maybe you have already walked away emotionally.
Your body still goes to church, but your heart has been drifting.
You pray less.
You hide more.
You have learned how to look spiritually alive while becoming exhausted inside.
Maybe shame convinced you that after everything you have done, Jesus would not want you back.
Look again at the Gospel.
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
The Gospel is filled with people whose stories should have ended in ruin.
Then grace entered the sentence.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not pretend sin is harmless.
He pays its terrible price.
He does not call darkness light.
He enters the darkness and saves.
He does not merely improve scandals.
He redeems sinners.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe today the story of the Rich Young Ruler is not asking whether you are wealthy.
Maybe it is asking whether Jesus is worth more to you than whatever you are terrified of losing.
Bring it to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Repent.
Ask for mercy.
Ask Him to break the grip of whatever has become your functional god.
If you need words, let them be simple:

“Jesus, I have loved something more than You. Forgive me. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to surrender what I keep protecting. Be Lord over the places I have kept locked. I want You more than the thing that owns me.”
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
But because sometimes bringing a struggle into the light is the first public refusal to keep pretending.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that grace still walks into ruined stories.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Not as a religious performance. Not to prove that you love God.
But if this biblical message helped you see Christ more clearly, sharing it can become a simple act of witness.

Supporting Gospel work is one practical way believers can participate in spreading biblical teaching, but it should always flow from willing generosity and love for Christ—not guilt, pressure, or an attempt to earn anything from God.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with following Jesus.
You can buy every Christian book in the store and still need Jesus.
You can wear the shirt and still need Jesus.
You can share the article and still need Jesus.
The Rich Young Ruler teaches us something far too important to bury beneath marketing:
Jesus Himself must remain the treasure.
Everything else is secondary.
Everything.
Because one day your money will belong to somebody else.
Your title will belong to somebody else.
Your house will belong to somebody else.
Your possessions will scatter.
Your photographs will fade.
People who once knew your voice will eventually be gone.
And the question will no longer be what you managed to accumulate.
The question will be whether all those temporary treasures kept you from the eternal Treasure standing in front of you saying:
“Follow Me.”
The Rich Young Ruler ran to Jesus.
Knelt before Jesus.
Spoke respectfully to Jesus.
Asked Jesus about eternal life.
Received a loving answer from Jesus.
And still walked away.
Sad.
Do not let familiarity with Jesus become a substitute for surrender to Jesus.
Do not settle for being almost persuaded.
Do not protect the very chain Christ is offering to break.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the idol.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the reputation.
Bring Him the money.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the thing you cannot imagine surrendering.
And discover that the hands asking you to release it are the same hands that were pierced to redeem sinners.
Do not spend your life clutching something that will eventually leave your hands while walking away from the One who was willing to stretch out His hands on a cross for you.
